knowledge_statements.title: Inhomogeneous Polynomial Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines affine positivity without imposing homogeneity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), with no requirement that its monomials have equal degree. The polynomial \(p\) is nonnegative on \(K\) when \(p(x)\ge 0\) for every \(x\in K\), and it is strictly positive on \(K\) when \(p(x)>0\) for every \(x\in K\). Whole-space positivity is obtained by taking \(K=\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inhomogeneous polynomial is nonnegative or strictly positive on a set when its value has the corresponding sign at every point of that set.

notation.meaning: affine domain on which positivity is tested

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Form Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard whole-space notion for real forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A form of degree \(d\) is a polynomial \(F\in\mathbb{R}[X_0,\ldots,X_n]\) satisfying \(F(\lambda X)=\lambda^dF(X)\) for all \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\). It is nonnegative when \(F(X)\ge 0\) for every \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\), and positive definite when \(F(X)>0\) for every \(X\ne 0\). A nonzero nonnegative form necessarily has even degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous form is nonnegative everywhere if it never takes a negative value; it is positive definite if equality occurs only at the origin.

children.title: Homogenization Maps
children.top_down_role: Passage from affine polynomials to homogeneous forms, including degree choices and added coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogenization Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives degree-preserving affine-to-homogeneous conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le d}p_\alpha x^\alpha\) have degree at most \(d\). Its degree-\(d\) homogenization is the form
\[p^{h}(X_0,X)=X_0^d p(X/X_0)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le d}p_\alpha X^\alpha X_0^{d-|\alpha|}.\]
The polynomial identity on the right defines \(p^h\) also when \(X_0=0\), and dehomogenization in the chart \(X_0=1\) recovers \(p(x)=p^h(1,x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenization adds one variable and powers it so every monomial has degree d; setting that variable to one recovers the original polynomial.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-to-homogeneous polynomial representation using one additional variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $p(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le d}c_\alpha x^\alpha\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ have degree $d$. Its homogenization is
\[
\bar p(x_1,\ldots,x_n,x_{n+1})=\sum_{|\alpha|\le d}c_\alpha x^\alpha x_{n+1}^{d-|\alpha|}=x_{n+1}^d p\!\left(\frac{x_1}{x_{n+1}},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_{n+1}}\right),
\]
where the final expression is understood through the displayed polynomial expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The homogenization of a degree-d polynomial adds one variable and multiplies each monomial by the power needed to make every term have total degree d.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar p(x,x_{n+1})=\sum_{|\alpha|\le d}c_\alpha x^\alpha x_{n+1}^{d-|\alpha|}\text{ is homogeneous of degree }d.

knowledge_statements.title: Positivity Transfer Across Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States whole-space positivity transfer for even-degree homogenization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) have even degree \(d\), and let \(p^h\) be its degree-\(d\) homogenization. Then
\[p(x)\ge0\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p^h(X_0,X)\ge0\text{ for all }(X_0,X)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}.\]
For \(X_0\ne0\), this follows from \(p^h(X_0,X)=X_0^d p(X/X_0)\); values on \(X_0=0\) are included by polynomial continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For even degree, a polynomial is globally nonnegative exactly when its homogenization is nonnegative in all homogeneous variables, including the hyperplane at infinity.

notation.meaning: homogenization of p at its even degree

children.title: Homogenizing-Hyperplane Behavior
children.top_down_role: Boundary phenomena occurring where the homogenizing coordinate vanishes.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogenizing-Hyperplane Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the restriction at infinity with the leading form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write \(p=p_0+p_1+\cdots+p_d\), where each \(p_k\) is homogeneous of degree \(k\) and \(p_d\ne0\). For the degree-\(d\) homogenization,
\[p^h(X_0,X)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}X_0^{d-k}p_k(X),\qquad p^h(0,X)=p_d(X).\]
Thus zeros, nonnegativity, or strict positivity of \(p^h\) on the homogenizing hyperplane \(X_0=0\), away from the origin, are exactly those of the leading form \(p_d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the homogenizing hyperplane, all lower-degree terms vanish and the homogenized polynomial equals the original polynomial’s highest-degree homogeneous part.

knowledge_statements.title: Positivity at Infinity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses positive definiteness of the leading form as the strict regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) have degree \(d\) and leading homogeneous form \(p_d\). The polynomial is positive at infinity when
\[p_d(u)>0\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}.\]
Equivalently, \(p_d\) has a positive minimum on the unit sphere. Under this condition \(d\) is even and \(p(x)\to+\infty\) as \(\lVert x\rVert\to\infty\); hence \(p\) is coercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is positive at infinity when its leading form is positive in every nonzero direction; this makes the polynomial tend to positive infinity radially.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Positive Polynomials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes pointwise strict positivity from uniform positive margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a polynomial \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is strictly positive on \(K\) if
\[p(x)>0\qquad\text{for every }x\in K.\]
If \(K\) is compact, strict positivity is equivalent to the existence of \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(p(x)\ge\varepsilon\) for every \(x\in K\). On a noncompact set, pointwise strict positivity need not provide such a uniform margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is strictly positive on a set if every value is positive; compactness additionally yields one positive lower bound valid everywhere on the set.

notation.meaning: uniform positive margin when it exists

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Coefficient Representation on the Nonnegative Orthant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous forms strictly positive on the nonnegative orthant away from the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a form such that \(f(x)>0\) whenever \(x_i\ge 0\) for all \(i\) and \(\sum_i x_i>0\). Then \(f=g/h\) for forms \(g\) and \(h\) having positive coefficients. In particular, for some \(r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\), one may choose \(h=(x_1+\cdots+x_n)^r\), so \((x_1+\cdots+x_n)^r f\) has positive coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous polynomial strictly positive on the nonnegative orthant away from the origin becomes a positive-coefficient form after multiplication by some nonnegative integer power of the coordinate sum.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Polynomials with Real Zeros
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the boundary regime of nonnegativity with attained zeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a polynomial \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is nonnegative on \(K\) with real zeros when
\[p(x)\ge0\text{ for every }x\in K,\qquad Z_K(p):=\{x\in K:p(x)=0\}\ne\varnothing.\]
If \(K=\mathbb{R}^n\), every point \(z\in Z_K(p)\) is a global minimizer of \(p\) with minimum value zero; if \(p\) is differentiable, then \(\nabla p(z)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime consists of nonnegative polynomials whose zero set meets the domain; each whole-space zero is a global minimizer with value zero.

notation.meaning: real zero set of p within K

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strict positivity away from the unavoidable homogeneous zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A real homogeneous form \(F\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is positive definite when
\[F(x)>0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}.\]
Equivalently, \(F(0)=0\) and the restriction of \(F\) to the unit sphere has a strictly positive minimum. Every nonzero positive-definite form has even degree and is nonnegative on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous form is positive definite when it is positive at every nonzero point; its only real zero is then the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Nonnegative Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines nonnegative forms having a nontrivial real projective zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonzero homogeneous form \(F\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is singular nonnegative when
\[F(x)\ge0\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\quad\text{and}\quad F(z)=0\text{ for some }z\ne0.\]
Every such nonzero zero is a global minimizer. Consequently \(\nabla F(z)=0\), so the projective hypersurface defined by \(F=0\) is singular at the projective point represented by \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular nonnegative form is nonnegative everywhere but has a nonzero real zero, which is necessarily a critical zero and a projective singularity.

children.title: Univariate Positivity on the Whole Line

knowledge_statements.title: Univariate Positivity on the Whole Line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the real sum-of-two-squares characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x]\). Then
\[p(x)\ge0\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb{R}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p(x)=a(x)^2+b(x)^2\text{ for some }a,b\in\mathbb{R}[x].\]
Equivalently, in the real factorization of a nonzero \(p\), its leading coefficient is positive and every real root has even multiplicity. In particular, every globally nonnegative univariate polynomial is a sum of squares of real polynomials; the zero polynomial is covered by \(a=b=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real univariate polynomial is nonnegative on the whole line exactly when it is a sum of two polynomial squares, equivalently all real roots have even multiplicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Form Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite real quadratic forms and their linear-square representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx\) for \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), where \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\). Then \(q(x)\ge 0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) if and only if \(Q\succeq0\). Equivalently, there exist vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\in\mathbb R^n\), with \(r=\operatorname{rank}Q\), such that \[q(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}(a_j^{\mathsf T}x)^2.\] Strict positivity for every nonzero \(x\) is equivalent to \(Q\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real quadratic form is globally nonnegative exactly when its symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite, equivalently when it is a sum of squares of linear forms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\ge0\text{ on }\mathbb R^n\iff Q\succeq0\iff q\text{ is a sum of squares of linear forms}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Form Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert’s binary-form case for real homogeneous forms of even degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[x,y]\) be homogeneous of degree \(2m\). Then \(f(x,y)\ge0\) for every \((x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\) if and only if there exist homogeneous forms \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\in\mathbb R[x,y]\) of degree \(m\) satisfying \[f(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}g_j(x,y)^2.\] Thus, for binary forms of every even degree, nonnegativity and sum-of-squares representability coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative real binary form of even degree is a sum of squares of real forms of half that degree, and every such sum is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\ge0\text{ on }\mathbb R^2\iff f=\sum_j g_j^2\) with \(\deg g_j=m\).

notation.meaning: half the degree of the binary form
real homogeneous forms of degree m

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary-form theorem is standard and precisely stated, but no citation or inspectable theorem locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Ternary Form Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert’s exceptional ternary-quartic positivity regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,x_2,x_3]\) be a homogeneous quartic form. Then \(f(x)ge0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^3\) if and only if there exist homogeneous quadratic forms \(q_1,\ldots,q_r\) such that \[f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}q_j(x)^2.\] This equivalence is special to ternary degree two and degree four; for ternary even degrees at least six, nonnegative forms need not be sums of squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative ternary quartic is a sum of squares of quadratic forms, but this equivalence fails for ternary forms of even degree at least six.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\ge0\text{ on }\mathbb R^3\iff f=\sum_j q_j^2\) with \(\deg q_j=2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative locator is required for Hilbert's ternary-quartic theorem and its failure boundary. The expression `f(x)ge0` also contains a malformed comparison command that must be corrected to `f(x)\ge0`.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Dimensional Form Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the nonnegative-equals-SOS equivalence for quartic forms in four or more variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge4\), nonnegativity of a homogeneous quartic form does not imply a sum-of-squares representation. In four variables, the Choi–Lam form \[F(x)=x_1^2x_2^2+x_2^2x_3^2+x_3^2x_1^2+x_4^4-4x_1x_2x_3x_4\] satisfies \(F(x)ge0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^4\), but it is not a sum of squares of real quadratic forms. The same obstruction extends to larger dimensions by adjoining unused variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting with four variables, a nonnegative quartic need not be a sum of squares; the Choi–Lam quartic is a concrete counterexample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F	ext{ is nonnegative on }\mathbb R^4\text{ but is not SOS}\).

notation.meaning: a sum of squares of real polynomials

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The non-SOS assertion for the Choi–Lam quartic requires an authoritative counterexample locator. The expression `F(x)ge0` is also malformed and must use `\ge`.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Interval Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Markov–Lukács representations for univariate polynomials nonnegative on a closed interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a<b\) and let \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\). If \(\deg p\le 2m\), then \(p\ge 0\) on \([a,b]\) if and only if \[p=s_0+(x-a)(b-x)s_1,\] where \(s_0,s_1\) are sums of squares with \(\deg s_0\le 2m\) and \(\deg s_1\le 2m-2\). If \(\deg p\le 2m+1\), the equivalent representation is \[p=(x-a)s_0+(b-x)s_1,\] where \(s_0,s_1\) are sums of squares of degree at most \(2m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegativity on a compact interval has exact weighted sum-of-squares representations, with different endpoint weights in even- and odd-degree cases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\ge0\text{ on }[a,b]\) is equivalent to the parity-appropriate displayed weighted SOS representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Endpoint Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity and derivative-sign constraints at zeros of interval-nonnegative polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p
ot\equiv0\) be nonnegative on \([a,b]\). Every zero \(c\in(a,b)\) has even multiplicity \(2r\) and satisfies \(p^{(2r)}(c)>0\). If \(m_a\) is the order of a zero at \(a\), then \(p^{(m_a)}(a)>0\); no parity restriction is imposed. If \(m_b\) is the order of a zero at \(b\), then \((-1)^{m_b}p^{(m_b)}(b)>0\). Thus one-sided endpoints admit odd-order contact, unlike interior points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior zeros of an interval-nonnegative polynomial have even multiplicity, while endpoint zeros may have either parity subject to the appropriate one-sided derivative sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interior zeros have even order; endpoint zeros satisfy the displayed one-sided derivative-sign rules.

notation.meaning: orders of vanishing at the left and right endpoints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The endpoint multiplicity and derivative-sign property is mathematically plausible, but it has no citation. Its assumption also contains corrupted `\ge` and `\in` expressions.

children.title: Half-Line Asymptotic Behavior
children.top_down_role: Interaction between ray positivity and behavior toward the unbounded end.

knowledge_statements.title: Half-Line Asymptotic Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leading-term constraints imposed by nonnegativity on a right half-line for nonconstant polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x)=c_dx^d+\cdots+c_0\) be a real polynomial of degree \(d\ge 1\). If \(p(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\ge a\), then \(c_d>0\) and \(p(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\to+\infty\); the degree \(d\) may be even or odd. Conversely, \(c_d>0\) guarantees eventual positivity: there exists \(R\in\mathbb R\) such that \(p(x)>0\) for all \(x\ge R\), though it does not guarantee nonnegativity on the entire prescribed ray \([a,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonconstant polynomial, right-ray nonnegativity forces a positive leading coefficient but no degree parity; a positive leading coefficient ensures only eventual, not whole-ray, positivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\ge0\text{ on }[a,\infty)\Rightarrow c_d>0\), while \(c_d>0\Rightarrow p>0\) on some terminal ray.

children.title: Orthant Positivity
children.top_down_role: Positivity over nonnegative coordinate regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthant Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of polynomial positivity on the nonnegative orthant to global even-substitution positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p	u00a0in\mathbb R[x_1,ldots,x_n]\), and define \(q(y)=p(y_1^2,ldots,y_n^2)\). Because the map \(y\mapsto(y_1^2,ldots,y_n^2)\) has image \(\mathbb R_+^n\), \[p(x)ge0\text{ for every }x	u00a0in\mathbb R_+^n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad q(y)ge0\text{ for every }y	u00a0in\mathbb R^n.\] This equivalence concerns nonnegativity itself; it does not assert that either polynomial possesses a sum-of-squares representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthant nonnegativity is equivalent to global nonnegativity after replacing every variable by its square, without implying sum-of-squares representability.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The even-variable substitution equivalence is correct and fits the leaf, but no source locator is supplied and several TeX commands are corrupted.

children.title: Coordinate-Face Regimes
children.top_down_role: Positivity behavior on coordinate faces and lower-dimensional orthant strata.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Face Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stratification of orthant positivity by relative interiors of coordinate faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). For each \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \[F_I=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:x_i>0\text{ for }i\in I,\ x_j=0\text{ for }j\notin I\}.\] These strata form a disjoint partition of \(\mathbb R_+^n\). For nonempty \(I\), define \(p_I((x_i)_{i\in I})=p(x_I,0_{I^c})\); for \(I=\varnothing\), set \(p_\varnothing=p(0)\) and regard \(\mathbb R_{++}^{\varnothing}\) as a singleton. Then \(p\) is nonnegative on \(\mathbb R_+^n\) if and only if \(p_I\) is nonnegative on \(\mathbb R_{++}^{I}\) for every \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthant positivity is equivalent to nonnegativity on every coordinate-face stratum, including the origin as the empty-face case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\ge0\text{ on }\mathbb R_+^n\iff p_I\ge0\text{ on }\mathbb R_{++}^{I}\text{ for every }I\), with the stated empty-set convention.

restriction obtained by zeroing coordinates outside I

children.title: Simplex Positivity
children.top_down_role: Positivity over affine or standard simplices.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous reduction of orthant positivity to positivity on the standard simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be homogeneous of degree \(d\), and let \(\Delta_{n-1}=\{u\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_i u_i=1\}\). For every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb R_+^n\), set \(t=\sum_i x_i>0\) and \(u=x/t\in\Delta_{n-1}\). Homogeneity gives \[f(x)=t^d f(u).\] Consequently, \(f\ge0\) on \(\mathbb R_+^n\) if and only if \(f\ge0\) on \(\Delta_{n-1}\); likewise, positivity away from the origin is equivalent to strict positivity on the simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a homogeneous form, positivity on the nonnegative orthant is completely determined by positivity on the standard simplex through radial normalization.

notation.meaning: the sum of the coordinates of a nonzero orthant point

children.title: Barycentric Boundary Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Barycentric Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-face stratification of simplex positivity in barycentric coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the standard simplex in barycentric coordinates as \(\Delta_{n-1}=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\). For each nonempty \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define its face stratum by \[G_I=\{\lambda\in\Delta_{n-1}:\lambda_i>0\text{ for }i\in I,\ \lambda_j=0\text{ for }j\notin I\}.\] The strata \(G_I\) partition the simplex. Therefore, a polynomial \(p\) is nonnegative on \(\Delta_{n-1}\) exactly when, for every nonempty \(I\), the restriction \(p_I=p|_{\lambda_j=0\text{ for }j\notin I}\) is nonnegative on \(G_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simplex positivity can be checked stratum by stratum: each boundary regime is obtained by setting the complementary barycentric coordinates to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\ge0\text{ on }\Delta_{n-1}\iff p_I\ge0\text{ on }G_I\text{ for every nonempty }I\).

notation.meaning: relative interior of the simplex face indexed by I
barycentric restriction of p to the indexed face

children.title: Sphere Positivity

knowledge_statements.title: Sphere Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegativity and strict positivity of a polynomial restricted to the real unit sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[x_0,\ldots,x_n]\) and \(S^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:\|x\|_2=1\}\). The polynomial \(f\) is nonnegative on the sphere when \(f(x)\ge 0\) for every \(x\in S^n\), and it is positive on the sphere when \(f(x)>0\) for every \(x\in S^n\). Equivalently, these conditions are \(\min_{x\in S^n}f(x)\ge0\) and \(\min_{x\in S^n}f(x)>0\), respectively, because \(S^n\) is compact and \(f\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sphere positivity means that a polynomial is nonnegative, or strictly positive, at every unit vector.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and compactness equivalence are mathematically precise and fit the leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Projective Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positivity of an even-degree homogeneous form on real projective space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\in\mathbb R[x_0,\ldots,x_n]\) be homogeneous of even degree \(2d\). Since \(F(\lambda x)=\lambda^{2d}F(x)\) for every \(\lambda
e0\), the sign of \(F(x)\) depends only on the projective point \([x]\in\mathbb{RP}^n\). The form is projectively nonnegative when \(F(x)\ge0\) for every \(x
e0\), and projectively positive when \(F(x)>0\) for every \(x
e0\). These conditions are equivalent to nonnegativity and positivity, respectively, of \(F\) on \(S^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An even-degree form is projectively positive precisely when it is positive on every nonzero representative, equivalently on the unit sphere.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a real homogeneous form of degree \(2d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\ge0\) on \(\mathbb{RP}^n\iff F|_{S^n}\ge0\), with the analogous strict equivalence.

notation.meaning: projective class of a nonzero vector

children.title: Antipodal Symmetry Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Antipodal Symmetry Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity determines whether a homogeneous form defines sign-invariant projective positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is a real homogeneous form of degree \(m\), then \(F(-x)=(-1)^mF(x)\) for every \(x\in S^n\). Thus even-degree forms are antipodally invariant and their values descend to \(\mathbb{RP}^n\). Odd-degree forms are antipodally anti-invariant; consequently, an odd-degree form that is nonnegative everywhere on \(S^n\) must vanish identically on \(S^n\), and hence must be the zero form. Therefore nontrivial scalar projective positivity is an even-degree regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even forms have equal values at antipodes and descend projectively; an odd form nonnegative on the whole sphere must be zero.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The antipodal parity property and odd-degree consequence are correct and appropriately classified as a property, but they lack cited evidence.

children.title: Homogeneous Chart Transitions
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of positivity information across projective affine charts.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Chart Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dehomogenized chart representations and their sign-compatible overlap transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be homogeneous of degree \(m\), and let \(U_i=\{[x]\in\mathbb{RP}^n:x_i\ne0\}\). Writing \(y_k=x_k/x_i\) for \(k\ne i\) gives the dehomogenization \(f_i(y)=F(y_0,\ldots,1,\ldots,y_n)\) and \(F(x)=x_i^m f_i(y)\). On \(U_i\cap U_j\), the corresponding local representatives satisfy \(f_j(z)=(x_i/x_j)^m f_i(y)\). Hence their signs agree on overlaps when \(m\) is even, so positivity is independent of the chosen homogeneous chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dehomogenizations differ on chart overlaps by a nonzero scaling factor; for even degree that factor is positive, preserving signs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_j(z)=(x_i/x_j)^m f_i(y)\), and even \(m\) makes chartwise positivity invariant.

notation.meaning: projective chart where the i-th coordinate is nonzero
dehomogenization of the form in chart i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chart-transition formula and even-degree sign invariance are correct and fit a representation leaf, but no source is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Positivity on Real Varieties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial nonnegativity modulo equality constraints on a real algebraic variety.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For polynomials \(h_1,\ldots,h_s\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), let \(V_{\mathbb R}(h)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h_1(x)=\cdots=h_s(x)=0\}\). A polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is nonnegative on this real variety when \(f(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\in V_{\mathbb R}(h)\), and strictly positive when \(f(x)>0\) there. The property depends only on the residue class of \(f\) modulo the vanishing ideal \(I(V_{\mathbb R}(h))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is positive on a real variety when its value is positive at every real common zero of the defining equations.

notation.meaning: real common zero set of the defining polynomials

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Square Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite sums of squares in a real polynomial ring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is a sum-of-squares polynomial if there exist an integer \(r\ge0\) and polynomials \(q_1,\ldots,q_r\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) such that \[f=\sum_{i=1}^{r}q_i^2.\] Every such decomposition certifies \(f(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Bounded SOS Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex cones of SOS polynomials with a fixed degree ceiling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n,d\in\mathbb N_0\), define \[\Sigma_{n,2d}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{r}q_i^2:r\in\mathbb N_0,\ q_i\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\ \deg q_i\le d\right\}.\] This is a convex cone contained in the vector space \(\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]_{\le2d}\) and in the cone of polynomials nonnegative on \(\mathbb R^n\). It is closed under addition and multiplication by nonnegative scalars.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Length SOS Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least number of polynomial squares representing a given SOS polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\in\Sigma_{n,2d}\), its SOS length is \[\ell_{\mathrm{SOS}}(f)=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb N_0:f=\sum_{i=1}^{r}q_i^2,\ \deg q_i\le d\right\}.\] If \(v_d(x)\) is the vector of monomials of degree at most \(d\), then equivalently \[\ell_{\mathrm{SOS}}(f)=\min\{\operatorname{rank}Q:f=v_d^{\mathsf T}Qv_d,\ Q\succeq0\}.\] A decomposition attaining this value is a minimal-length SOS decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SOS length is the fewest polynomial squares needed to represent an SOS polynomial, equivalently the minimum rank of a positive semidefinite Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{SOS}}(f)\) equals the minimum feasible Gram-matrix rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Dimension Length Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOS-length growth with the number of variables fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n\in\mathbb N_0\). For every \(d\in\mathbb N_0\) and every \(f\in\Sigma_{n,2d}\), a positive semidefinite Gram representation indexed by monomials of degree at most \(d\) yields \[\ell_{\mathrm{SOS}}(f)\le\binom{n+d}{n}.\] Consequently, with \(n\) fixed, the universal SOS-length bound grows as \(O(d^n)\) as \(d\to\infty\). children.title: Coefficient-Matching Constraints
children.top_down_role: Linear constraints connecting polynomial coefficients to Gram entries.

knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient-Matching Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear equations connecting polynomial coefficients to entries of a Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a monomial vector \(z(x)=(x^{\beta_1},\ldots,x^{\beta_N})^{\mathsf T}\), and let \(E:=\{\beta_i+\beta_j:1\le i,j\le N\}\cup\operatorname{supp}(p)\). Write \(p(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in E}p_\alpha x^\alpha\), taking \(p_\alpha=0\) for exponents absent from \(p\). A matrix \(Q\in\mathbb S^N\) represents \(p\) precisely when, for every \(\alpha\in E\), \[\sum_{i,j:\,\beta_i+\beta_j=\alpha}Q_{ij}=p_\alpha.\] Equivalently, the linear map \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^N\to\mathbb R^E\), defined by \(\mathcal A(Q)=(\operatorname{coeff}_{\alpha}(z^{\mathsf T}Qz))_{\alpha\in E}\), satisfies \(\mathcal A(Q)=(p_\alpha)_{\alpha\in E}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the finite set of exponents occurring in the polynomial or the Gram expansion, representing the polynomial imposes one linear equation on the Gram-matrix entries for each coefficient.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) is a fixed finite monomial vector.

notation.meaning: exponent vector of the i-th monomial in z
finite coefficient index set containing the supports of p and the Gram expansion
linear Gram coefficient map indexed by E

children.title: Positive-Semidefinite Gram Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite feasibility of Gram representatives satisfying coefficient constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Gram Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite feasibility condition for a coefficient-matched Gram representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(p\) and monomial vector \(z\), let \(b=\operatorname{coeff}(p)\) and \(\mathcal A(Q)=\operatorname{coeff}(z^{\mathsf T}Qz)\). Gram feasibility is the conic system \[\text{find }Q\in\mathbb S^N\quad\text{such that}\quad \mathcal A(Q)=b,\qquad Q\succeq0.\] A feasible \(Q\) yields an SOS decomposition by any factorization \(Q=V^{\mathsf T}V\). Conversely, every SOS decomposition whose summands lie in \(\operatorname{span}z\) produces such a feasible matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gram feasibility requires simultaneous satisfaction of coefficient equations and positive semidefiniteness; a feasible factorization directly yields an SOS decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) and the monomial vector \(z\) are fixed.
\(\mathcal A\) is the associated coefficient map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists Q\succeq0:\mathcal A(Q)=b\) exactly when \(p\) has an SOS decomposition supported by \(z\).

children.title: Affine-Slice Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency of the affine Gram slice before positivity restrictions are imposed.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Slice Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency criterion for the affine space of coefficient-matched Gram matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^N\to\mathbb R^M\) be the Gram coefficient map and \(b=\operatorname{coeff}(p)\). The coefficient equations are consistent if and only if \(b\in\operatorname{range}\mathcal A\). If \(Q_0\) is one solution, then every symmetric solution and only such a solution has the form \[Q=Q_0+H,\qquad H\in\ker\mathcal A.\] Thus the coefficient-matched matrices form the affine slice \(Q_0+\ker\mathcal A\); Gram feasibility additionally requires this slice to intersect \(\mathbb S^N_+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consistent coefficient equations form a translate of the coefficient map's kernel; SOS feasibility requires that affine slice to meet the PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A^{-1}(b)\neq\varnothing\iff b\in\operatorname{range}\mathcal A\), and then \(\mathcal A^{-1}(b)=Q_0+\ker\mathcal A\).

children.title: Gram Infeasibility Sources
children.top_down_role: Structural causes preventing a coefficient-matched positive-semidefinite representative.

knowledge_statements.title: Gram Infeasibility Sources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive algebraic-versus-conic failure split for a fixed Gram model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(z\), \(\mathcal A\), and target coefficient vector \(b\), the Gram system \(\mathcal A(Q)=b\), \(Q\succeq0\) is infeasible in either of two regimes. Algebraic inconsistency occurs when \(b\notin\operatorname{range}\mathcal A\). Otherwise, choosing \(Q_0\in\mathcal A^{-1}(b)\), conic incompatibility occurs when \[(Q_0+\ker\mathcal A)\cap\mathbb S^N_+=\varnothing.\] Hence failure may arise from inadequate monomial support or from the absence of a PSD matrix among coefficient-matched representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gram infeasibility means either the coefficient equations have no solution or their affine solution set never intersects the PSD cone.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) and its coefficient map \(\mathcal A\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{Q:\mathcal A(Q)=b,\ Q\succeq0\}=\varnothing\) precisely under algebraic inconsistency or conic incompatibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Gram Slices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine family of symmetric matrices representing one polynomial in a fixed basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a polynomial \(p\), a monomial vector \(z\), and the coefficient map \(\mathcal A(Q)=\operatorname{coeff}(z^{\mathsf T}Qz)\), the affine Gram slice is \[\mathcal L_p:=\{Q\in\mathbb S^N:\mathcal A(Q)=\operatorname{coeff}(p)\}.\] When nonempty, \(\mathcal L_p=Q_0+\ker\mathcal A\) for any \(Q_0\in\mathcal L_p\). Its positive-semidefinite section \(\mathcal G_p:=\mathcal L_p\cap\mathbb S^N_+\) is the Gram spectrahedron of \(p\) relative to \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine Gram slice contains all symmetric matrices representing a fixed polynomial; intersecting it with the PSD cone gives the Gram spectrahedron.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) and the finite monomial vector \(z\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L_p=\mathcal A^{-1}(\operatorname{coeff}(p))\) and \(\mathcal G_p=\mathcal L_p\cap\mathbb S^N_+\).

children.title: Facial Strata of Gram Spectrahedra
children.top_down_role: Organization of Gram spectrahedra by nested faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial Strata of Gram Spectrahedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces induced by kernel subspaces of positive-semidefinite Gram matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G_p=\mathcal L_p\cap\mathbb S^N_+\). For a subspace \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^N\), define \[F_U:=\{Q\in\mathcal G_p:U\subseteq\ker Q\}.\] Whenever nonempty, \(F_U\) is a face of \(\mathcal G_p\), obtained by intersecting \(\mathcal L_p\) with the PSD-cone face \(\{Q\succeq0:U\subseteq\ker Q\}\). Conversely, every face of \(\mathcal G_p\) equals \(F_U\) for the common-kernel subspace \(U=\bigcap_{Q\in F}\ker Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of a Gram spectrahedron are indexed by subspaces forced into the kernels of all matrices on the face.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) denotes a nonempty face when the converse is invoked.

notation.meaning: Gram face determined by kernel subspace U

children.title: Extreme Gram Matrices

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Gram Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-space criterion for extremality in an affine Gram spectrahedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathcal G_p\) and let \(R=\operatorname{range}Q\). Then \(Q\) is an extreme point of \(\mathcal G_p\) if and only if the only \(H\in\ker\mathcal A\) satisfying \(H=P_RHP_R\) is \(H=0\), where \(P_R\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(R\). Equivalently, the translation space of the affine Gram slice has trivial intersection with the linear span of the minimal PSD-cone face containing \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gram matrix is extreme exactly when no nonzero coefficient-preserving perturbation remains supported on its range.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is the Gram coefficient map.

children.title: Rank Profiles on Gram Faces
children.top_down_role: Variation of Gram rank across facial strata.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Profiles on Gram Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank behavior within the relative interior and boundary of a Gram face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(\mathcal G_p\), and set \(U_F=\bigcap_{Q\in F}\ker Q\). Every matrix in \(\operatorname{relint}F\) has kernel exactly \(U_F\), hence constant rank \(N-\dim U_F\). Every \(Q\in F\) satisfies \(U_F\subseteq\ker Q\), so \(\operatorname{rank}Q\le N-\dim U_F\). A strict rank drop therefore places \(Q\) in the relative boundary of \(F\), within a proper subface determined by its enlarged kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank is constant and maximal on a Gram face's relative interior; boundary subfaces arise when the kernel enlarges and rank drops.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a nonempty face of a Gram spectrahedron in \(\mathbb S^N\).

notation.meaning: common kernel of matrices in F

children.title: Degenerate Facial Regimes
children.top_down_role: Faces exhibiting singularity, dimension collapse, or boundary-only behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Facial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of strict feasibility and confinement to a proper PSD face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G_p=\{Q\succeq0:\mathcal A(Q)=b\}\) be nonempty. The Gram system is facially degenerate when it has no positive-definite feasible matrix. Equivalently, there exists a nonzero subspace \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^N\) such that \[U\subseteq\ker Q\quad\text{for every }Q\in\mathcal G_p.\] In this regime \(\mathcal G_p\) lies in the proper PSD-cone face determined by \(U\); its relative geometry must be studied in that face rather than in the full cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gram spectrahedron is facially degenerate when all feasible matrices share a nontrivial kernel, so the set lies in a proper PSD face.

knowledge_statements.title: Gram-Rank Strata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition of a Gram spectrahedron by matrix rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Gram spectrahedron \(\mathcal G_p\subseteq\mathbb S^N_+\), its rank-\(r\) stratum is \[\mathcal G_p^{(r)}:=\{Q\in\mathcal G_p:\operatorname{rank}Q=r\},\qquad 0\le r\le N.\] The nonempty strata form a disjoint partition of \(\mathcal G_p\). If \(Q\in\mathcal G_p^{(r)}\) and \(Q=V^{\mathsf T}V\) with \(V\) having \(r\) rows, then \(Q\) yields an SOS representation with \(r\) squares; the minimum feasible Gram rank equals the minimum number of squares supported by the chosen monomial vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gram-rank strata group feasible Gram matrices by rank, which corresponds to the number of squares in a minimal factorization.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G_p\) is defined relative to a fixed monomial vector of length \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal G_p=\bigsqcup_{r=0}^N\mathcal G_p^{(r)}\), with rank \(r\) giving an \(r\)-square Gram factorization.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Gram Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative boundary criterion for a nonempty affine slice of the PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G_p=\mathcal L_p\cap\mathbb S^N_+\) be nonempty, and let \(U=\bigcap_{Q\in\mathcal G_p}\ker Q\). Put \(R=U^\perp\). Then \(Q\in\operatorname{relint}\mathcal G_p\) exactly when the restriction \(Q|_R\) is positive definite. Consequently, \(Q\) lies on the relative boundary of \(\mathcal G_p\) exactly when \(\ker Q\) strictly contains \(U\). Under strict feasibility, \(U=\{0\}\), so boundary matrices are precisely the singular feasible Gram matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-boundary Gram matrices have kernels larger than the spectrahedron's common kernel; with strict feasibility, they are exactly the singular feasible matrices.
assumptions_latex: Relative interior and boundary are taken in \(\operatorname{aff}\mathcal G_p\).

notation.meaning: common kernel of the Gram spectrahedron
effective range space of the minimal containing PSD face

children.title: Kernel Geometry of the Gram Map

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Geometry of the Gram Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine geometry of Gram matrices in a fixed polynomial basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z(x)=(z_1(x),\ldots,z_m(x))^\top\) be a linearly independent polynomial vector, and define the linear Gram map \(\mathcal A_z:\mathbb S^m\to\mathbb R[x]\) by \(\mathcal A_z(Q)=z(x)^\top Qz(x)\). If \(Q_0\) represents \(p\), then every symmetric Gram representative of \(p\) is obtained by adding an element of the kernel: \[\mathcal A_z^{-1}(p)=Q_0+\ker\mathcal A_z.\] Hence the positive-semidefinite Gram spectrahedron is \[\mathcal G_z(p)=(Q_0+\ker\mathcal A_z)\cap\mathbb S_+^m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All Gram matrices representing a fixed polynomial form an affine translate of the Gram-map kernel; SOS representatives are its intersection with the positive semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_z^{-1}(p)=Q_0+\ker\mathcal A_z\) and \(\mathcal G_z(p)=\mathcal A_z^{-1}(p)\cap\mathbb S_+^m\).

notation.meaning: Real symmetric matrices of order m.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Gram Representatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for nonuniqueness of symmetric and positive-semidefinite Gram representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a polynomial vector \(z\), define \(\mathcal A_z(Q)=z^\top Qz\) on \(\mathbb S^m\), and suppose \(p=z^\top Q_0z\) for some \(Q_0\in\mathbb S^m\). A symmetric matrix represents \(p\) exactly when it has the form \(Q_0+N\) with \(N\in\ker\mathcal A_z\). Thus \(p\) has multiple symmetric Gram representatives if and only if \(\ker\mathcal A_z\ne\{0\}\). If additionally \(Q_0\succeq0\), then \(p\) has a positive-semidefinite Gram representative distinct from \(Q_0\) if and only if there exists \(N\in\ker\mathcal A_z\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(Q_0+N\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric Gram nonuniqueness occurs exactly along nonzero kernel directions. Starting from a PSD representative, PSD nonuniqueness additionally requires a nonzero kernel perturbation that remains PSD.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) has a PSD Gram representative distinct from \(Q_0\) if and only if \(\exists N\in\ker\mathcal A_z\setminus\{0\}\) with \(Q_0+N\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: Gram map for the fixed polynomial vector.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS Decomposition Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence between PSD Gram matrices and SOS decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)^\top\) span a finite-dimensional polynomial space. A polynomial \(p\) admits a representation \(p=z^\top Qz\) with \(Q\succeq0\) if and only if there exist polynomials \(q_1,\ldots,q_r\in\operatorname{span}(z)\) such that \[p=\sum_{j=1}^r q_j^2.\] More precisely, every factorization \(Q=C^\top C\) yields \(q=Cz\), while the coefficient rows of any such SOS decomposition form a matrix \(C\) whose Gram matrix \(C^\top C\) represents \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial has a PSD Gram matrix in a basis exactly when it is a sum of squares of polynomials from that basis span.

notation.meaning: Coefficient matrix of the square polynomials in basis z.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Variation Across Representatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gram rank may vary along the feasible affine kernel slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linearly independent finite polynomial vector \(z\), let \(\mathcal G_z(p)=\{Q\in\mathbb S_+^m:z^\top Qz=p\}\) and assume \(\mathcal G_z(p)\ne\varnothing\). If \(Q\in\mathcal G_z(p)\) has rank \(r\), then there exists a compact factorization \(Q=C^\top C\) with \(C\in\mathbb R^{r\times m}\) of full row rank, yielding an SOS decomposition of \(p\) into \(r\) linearly independent square factors from \(\operatorname{span}(z)\). Conversely, every decomposition of \(p\) into \(k\) such squares yields a Gram matrix of rank at most \(k\). Hence \[\min_{Q\in\mathcal G_z(p)}\operatorname{rank}Q\] equals the minimum number of square terms in an SOS decomposition of \(p\) whose factors belong to \(\operatorname{span}(z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact factorization of a rank-r PSD Gram matrix gives r independent square factors, and the least Gram rank equals the fewest squares obtainable within the fixed basis span.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) is a linearly independent finite polynomial vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Full Monomial Bases

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For variables \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) and integer \(d\ge0\), the full monomial basis vector of degree at most \(d\) is \[v_d(x)=(x^\alpha)_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^n,\ |\alpha|\le d},\] in any fixed ordering. It contains \(\binom{n+d}{d}\) monomials and spans \(\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}\). Consequently every polynomial of degree at most \(2d\) lies in the linear span of the products of entries of \(v_d\), although it need not possess a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton-Polytope Support Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton-polytope restriction for square factors of an SOS polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\) be nonzero and suppose \(p=\sum_{j=1}^r q_j^2\). If \(P=\operatorname{Newt}(p)\) is the convex hull of the exponent support of \(p\), then every exponent occurring in every \(q_j\) belongs to \(\tfrac12P\cap\mathbb N^n\). Therefore an SOS Gram search may use the reduced monomial vector \[z_P(x)=(x^\alpha)_{\alpha\in(\frac12P)\,\cap\,\mathbb N^n}\] without excluding any SOS decomposition of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every monomial in an SOS factor lies in half the polynomial's Newton polytope, allowing a lossless reduction of the Gram basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Adapted Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block Gram representation induced by finite-group invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act linearly on a finite-dimensional polynomial space \(V\), and let \(p\) be \(G\)-invariant. If \(p=z^\top Qz\) for a \(G\)-stable basis vector \(z\) and some \(Q\succeq0\), then averaging gives \[\bar Q=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}\rho(g)^\top Q\rho(g)\succeq0,\qquad p=z^\top\bar Qz.\] In a basis decomposing \(V\) into isotypic components, \(\bar Q\) has the corresponding symmetry blocks, reducing the Gram feasibility problem to smaller PSD blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging produces an invariant Gram matrix, which becomes block structured in a basis adapted to the group representation.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and acts linearly on a polynomial space \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar Q\succeq0\), \(p=z^\top\bar Qz\), and \(\bar Q\) respects the isotypic decomposition of \(V\).

notation.meaning: Matrix representing the action of g on the chosen basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal Polynomial Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gram coordinates in a basis orthogonal for a chosen inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\subset\mathbb R[x]\) be finite dimensional and let \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\mu\) be an inner product on \(V\), for example \(\langle f,g\rangle_\mu=\int fg\,d\mu\) when the integral is positive definite on \(V\). An orthogonal polynomial basis is a vector \(\phi=(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m)^\top\) spanning \(V\) such that \(\langle\phi_i,\phi_j\rangle_\mu=0\) whenever \(i\ne j\). A Gram representation in this basis has the form \(p=\phi^\top Q_\phi\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonal polynomial basis consists of mutually orthogonal spanning polynomials under a specified inner product and supports Gram representations in those coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real polynomial space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\) is orthogonal iff it spans \(V\) and \(\langle\phi_i,\phi_j\rangle_\mu=0\) for \(i\ne j\).

notation.meaning: Gram matrix in the orthogonal basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Diagonally Scaled Monomial Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monomial Gram bases rescaled by nonzero diagonal weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v=(x^{\alpha_1},\ldots,x^{\alpha_m})^\top\) be a monomial vector and let \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\) with every \(d_i\ne0\). The diagonally scaled monomial basis is \(z=Dv\). It spans the same polynomial space as \(v\). If \(p=v^\top Q_vv\), then the same polynomial is represented in scaled coordinates by \[p=z^\top Q_zz,\qquad Q_z=D^{-\top}Q_vD^{-1}.\] Positive semidefiniteness and rank are preserved under this congruence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonzero diagonal scaling preserves the monomial span and transforms Gram matrices by an invertible congruence, preserving PSD status and rank.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a real invertible diagonal matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Dependent Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning changes under invertible polynomial-basis transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=T\phi\) for an invertible matrix \(T\), and represent the same polynomial by \(p=z^\top Q_zz=\phi^\top Q_\phi\phi\). Then \(Q_\phi=T^\top Q_zT\). Although feasibility and inertia are invariant under this congruence, Euclidean spectral conditioning is not. For nonsingular \(Q_z\), \[\kappa_2(Q_\phi)\le \kappa_2(T)^2\kappa_2(Q_z).\] Likewise, the coefficient matrix of the Gram linear equations changes with the basis, so its singular values and numerical conditioning can improve or deteriorate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing polynomial coordinates preserves exact Gram feasibility but can substantially alter matrix and linear-system conditioning.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_z\) is symmetric and nonsingular for the displayed condition-number bound.

notation.meaning: Gram matrices in the two bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Gram Coordinate Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Congruence rule for converting Gram matrices between bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\) and \(\phi\) be ordered bases of the same finite-dimensional polynomial space, related by \(z=T\phi\) with \(T\) invertible. Then \[z^\top Q_zz=\phi^\top(T^\top Q_zT)\phi.\] Thus conversion from \(z\)-coordinates to \(\phi\)-coordinates is \(Q_\phi=T^\top Q_zT\), while the inverse conversion is \(Q_z=T^{-\top}Q_\phi T^{-1}\). These maps are bijections between the corresponding Gram fibers and preserve positive semidefiniteness and rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gram matrices in two bases are converted by congruence, yielding a rank- and PSD-preserving bijection between their Gram fibers.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) and \(\phi\) are bases of the same polynomial space.

notation.meaning: Coordinate-change matrix from phi to z.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Functionals for SOS Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment-matrix characterization of the dual truncated SOS cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge1\) and \(d\ge0\) be integers, and let \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\subset\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]_{\le2d}\) be the cone of sums of squares of real polynomials of degree at most \(d\). Then \[L_y\in\Sigma_{n,2d}^*\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M_d(y)\succeq0.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Non-SOS Separating Witnesses

knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of a weak Gram system to its minimal PSD face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input the affine Gram slice \(\mathcal G(p)\). While its current affine system has no point in the relative interior of the current face \(F\subseteq\mathbb S_+^N\), find a nonzero exposing matrix \(Y\succeq0\) satisfying \(\langle Y,Q\rangle=0\) for every feasible \(Q\), and replace \(F\) by \(F\cap Y^\perp\). Stop when the reduced slice meets \(\operatorname{ri}F\); output the resulting minimal face and reduced Gram system.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal G(p)\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\ne\varnothing\), where \(F_{\min}\) is the minimal face containing all feasible Gram matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hilbert’s Nonnegative–SOS Exactness Regimes and the Motzkin Counterexample
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the extracted dimension-degree regimes of nonnegative–SOS equality and an explicit strict-inclusion witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The equality
\[
\Sigma_{n,d}=\mathcal Q_{n,d}
\]
holds if \(n=1\), if \(d=2\), or if \((n,d)=(2,4)\). The Motzkin polynomial
\[
M(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_1^4x_2^2+x_1^2x_2^4-3x_1^2x_2^2x_3^2+x_3^6
\]
has infimum \(0\), attained at \((1,1,1)\), and is nonnegative but not SOS; hence
\[
M\in\mathcal Q_{3,6}\setminus\Sigma_{3,6}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative and SOS cones coincide in the stated univariate, degree-two, and bivariate degree-four regimes. The degree-six Motzkin polynomial in three variables is nonnegative but not SOS.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert exactness case for homogeneous quadratic forms in arbitrary dimension.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(p\in P_{n,2d}\setminus\Sigma_{n,2d}\). Let \(v_d(x)\) contain all monomials of degree \(d\), and define \(\Sigma_{n,2d}=\{v_d(x)^{\mathsf T}Qv_d(x):Q\succeq0\}\). Then

For \(p\in\Sigma_{n,2d}\), let \(\mathcal G(p)=\{Q\succeq0:p(x)=v_d(x)^{\mathsf T}Qv_d(x)\}\). Then
\[
p\in\partial\Sigma_{n,2d}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathcal G(p)\cap\{Q:Q\succ0\}=\varnothing.

Equivalently, every positive-semidefinite Gram matrix representing a boundary SOS form is singular. This does not require the form to have a nonzero real zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Faces of the Nonnegative Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed faces obtained by prescribing real zeros on the unit sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any nonempty finite set \(Z\subset\mathbb S^{n-1}\), define
\[
F_Z=\{p\in P_{n,2d}:p(z)=0\text{ for every }z\in Z\}.
\]
Then \(F_Z\) is an exposed face of \(P_{n,2d}\), exposed by the nonnegative functional \(p\mapsto\sum_{z\in Z}p(z)\). In particular, if \(p\in P_{n,2d}\) has a nonzero zero \(z\), then \(p\) belongs to the proper exposed face \(F_{\{z/\|z\|_2\}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requiring nonnegative forms to vanish on specified sphere points produces exposed faces; every boundary form belongs to such a proper zero face.
assumptions_latex: \(n\geq 1\), \(d\geq 1\), and \(Z\subset\mathbb S^{n-1}\) is finite and nonempty.

notation.meaning: Face of nonnegative forms vanishing on Z.

knowledge_statements.title: Faces of the SOS Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces of the SOS cone viewed through their positive-semidefinite Gram lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L(Q)=v_d(x)^{\mathsf T}Qv_d(x)\), so that \(\Sigma_{n,2d}=L(\mathbb S_+^N)\). If \(F\) is a face of \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\), then
\[
\widehat F=\{Q\in\mathbb S_+^N:L(Q)\in F\}
\]
is a face of \(\mathbb S_+^N\), and \(F=L(\widehat F)\). Consequently there is a subspace \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^N\) such that \(\widehat F=\{Q\succeq0:\operatorname{range}Q\subseteq U\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of the SOS cone lifts to a positive-semidefinite face determined by a Gram-matrix range subspace, and projecting that lift recovers the face.
assumptions_latex: \(v_d\) is the full degree-d monomial vector of length \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat F\text{ is a face of }\mathbb S_+^N\text{ and }F=L(\widehat F)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R_+p\text{ is extreme in }P_{n,2d}\iff [p=f+g,\ f,g\in P_{n,2d}\Rightarrow f,g\in\mathbb R_+p]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic extremality condition inside the cone of nonnegative forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonzero form \(p\in P_{n,2d}\) generates an extreme ray of \(P_{n,2d}\) exactly when
\[
p=f+g,\quad f,g\in P_{n,2d}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f=\lambda p\text{ and }g=\mu p
\]
for some \(\lambda,\mu\geq0\). Equivalently, the smallest face of \(P_{n,2d}\) containing \(p\) is the ray \(\mathbb R_+p\).

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Extremality Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Size of the Cone Gap

knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient-Perturbation Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-degree coefficient approximation cannot remove a strict SOS gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[
\delta(p):=\inf_{s\in\Sigma_{n,2d}}\|p-s\|>0.
\]
Consequently no sequence of degree-\(2d\) SOS forms can converge coefficientwise to such a \(p\). In particular, for any fixed \(q\in H_{n,2d}\), the perturbation \(p+\varepsilon q\) remains outside \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\) whenever \(|\varepsilon|\,\|q\|<\delta(p)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Based Cone Distances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Point-to-cone and normalized-section distances in finite-dimensional coefficient spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(C,D\subset V\) be closed cones. Define
\[
\operatorname{dist}_{\|\cdot\|}(x,D)=\inf_{y\in D}\|x-y\|.
\]
Since unbounded cones generally have infinite Hausdorff distance, choose a continuous positive normalization \(\ell\) and compare compact bases \(C_1=\{x\in C:\ell(x)=1\}\) and \(D_1=\{y\in D:\ell(y)=1\}\) using
\[
d_H(C_1,D_1)=\max\left\{\sup_{x\in C_1}\operatorname{dist}(x,D_1),\sup_{y\in D_1}\operatorname{dist}(y,C_1)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone distances use point-to-cone norm distance or Hausdorff distance between compact normalized bases, because the Hausdorff distance between unbounded cones is usually infinite.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite-dimensional and \(C,D\subset V\) are closed cones.
\(\ell\) is strictly positive on each cone away from the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Volume Ratios of Cone Sections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the relative volume of compact normalized sections of the nonnegative and SOS cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(\Sigma\subseteq P\subseteq V\) be closed convex cones, and let \(\ell\in V^*\). Suppose the sections \(B_P=\{p\in P:\ell(p)=1\}\) and \(B_\Sigma=\{p\in\Sigma:\ell(p)=1\}\) are compact convex bodies in the same affine space of dimension \(m\). Their volume ratio and volume-radius ratio, computed using any common Lebesgue measure on that affine space, are respectively
\[
R_{\mathrm{vol}}(\Sigma,P;\ell)=\frac{\operatorname{vol}_m(B_\Sigma)}{\operatorname{vol}_m(B_P)},\qquad
R_{\mathrm{vr}}(\Sigma,P;\ell)=R_{\mathrm{vol}}(\Sigma,P;\ell)^{1/m}.
\]
Both ratios lie in \([0,1]\), and the quotient is independent of the common scaling of Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The volume ratio compares compact, equally normalized SOS and nonnegative cone sections; its dimension-normalized root compares their effective linear sizes.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite-dimensional and \(\Sigma\subseteq P\) are closed convex cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates genuine normalization dependence from invariance under simultaneous linear transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Sigma\subseteq P\subseteq V\) and \(\ell\in V^*\) satisfy the compact-section hypotheses. For an invertible linear map \(T:V\to V\), set \(P'=T(P)\), \(\Sigma'=T(\Sigma)\), and \(\ell'=\ell\circ T^{-1}\). Then \(T\) maps each normalized section bijectively onto its primed counterpart, and its common affine Jacobian cancels in the quotient. Hence
\[
R_{\mathrm{vol}}(\Sigma',P';\ell')=R_{\mathrm{vol}}(\Sigma,P;\ell).
\]
By contrast, replacing \(\ell\) by an unrelated normalization \(\widetilde\ell\) changes the radial scaling of the two cone sections pointwise; no equality between the resulting volume ratios follows without an automorphism transporting \((P,\Sigma,\ell)\) to \((P,\Sigma,\widetilde\ell)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Volume ratios are invariant under covariant linear coordinate changes, but generally depend on an independently changed normalization functional.
assumptions_latex: The original and transported normalized sections are compact and full-dimensional in their affine hulls.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Dimensional Comparison Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies sequences of normalized cone sections through their volume-radius ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(N\), let \(B_{\Sigma,N}\subseteq B_{P,N}\) be compact convex bodies of common affine dimension \(m_N\), and define
\[
\rho_N=\left(\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{m_N}(B_{\Sigma,N})}{\operatorname{vol}_{m_N}(B_{P,N})}\right)^{1/m_N}.
\]
The comparison is asymptotically volume-equivalent when \(\rho_N\to1\); it has a constant-factor volume-radius gap when \(\rho_N\to c\) for some \(c\in(0,1)\); and it exhibits volume-radius collapse when \(\rho_N\to0\). These regimes concern normalized linear size: the unrooted volume fraction equals \(\rho_N^{m_N}\), so it may vanish exponentially in \(m_N\) even when \(\rho_N\) remains bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: High-dimensional cone sections are compared by rooted volume ratios, distinguishing equivalence, a constant linear-size gap, and collapse.
assumptions_latex: \(B_{\Sigma,N}\subseteq B_{P,N}\) are compact and full-dimensional in a common \(m_N\)-dimensional affine space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_N\to1\), \(\rho_N\to c\in(0,1)\), and \(\rho_N\to0\) define the three comparison regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Dependent Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines worst-case normalized approximation error as ambient dimension and degree vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each index \(N\), let \((V_N,\|\cdot\|_N)\) be finite-dimensional, let \(\Sigma_N\subseteq P_N\subseteq V_N\) be cones, and choose a normalization \(\ell_N\) for which \(B_{P,N}=\{p\in P_N:\ell_N(p)=1\}\) and \(B_{\Sigma,N}=\{s\in\Sigma_N:\ell_N(s)=1\}\) are nonempty and compact. The dimension-dependent one-sided approximation error is
\[
\varepsilon_N=\sup_{p\in B_{P,N}}\inf_{s\in B_{\Sigma,N}}\|p-s\|_N.
\]
A family gives asymptotically uniform approximation precisely when \(\varepsilon_N\to0\). The sequence \((\varepsilon_N)\) depends on the norm and normalization, which must therefore remain specified when dimensions or polynomial degrees change.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Without Exact Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nested closed-cone example separates arbitrarily accurate approximation from finite-level membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\mathbb{R}_+^2\) with the Euclidean norm and, for each integer \(k\ge1\), let
\[
C_k=\operatorname{cone}\{(1,0),(1,k)\}.
\]
Then every \(C_k\) is a closed convex cone, \(C_k\subseteq C_{k+1}\subseteq P\), and \((0,1)\notin C_k\) for every finite \(k\). Nevertheless, with \(z_k=(1/k,1)=(1/k)(1,k)\), one has \(z_k\in C_k\) and
\[
\|z_k-(0,1)\|_2=1/k\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus convergence of approximants from an increasing cone hierarchy does not imply that the limit belongs to any finite hierarchy level, even when every level is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point can be approximated arbitrarily well by an increasing sequence of closed cones while belonging to none of them.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Function SOS Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert–Artin theorem over the real numbers for globally nonnegative polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). If \(f(a)\ge0\) for every \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\), then there exist finitely many rational functions \(r_1,\ldots,r_m\in\mathbb{R}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) such that
\[
f=\sum_{i=1}^{m}r_i^2
\]
as an identity in \(\mathbb{R}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). Conversely, every polynomial admitting such an identity is nonnegative at every real point where all displayed rational functions are defined; after cancellation, continuity of the polynomial extends nonnegativity to all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Thus global polynomial nonnegativity is equivalent to being a sum of squares in the rational function field.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real polynomial is globally nonnegative exactly when it is a finite sum of squares of real rational functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cleared-Denominator Representations

Let \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). \[
q^2f=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i^2.
\]
Equivalently, a polynomial is a sum of squares in the rational function field precisely when multiplication by the square of some nonzero polynomial makes it a polynomial SOS.

knowledge_statements.title: Pfister-Type Rational SOS Length
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds rational SOS length by the number of variables over a real closed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be real closed and let \(F=R(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). Every element of \(F\) that is a sum of finitely many squares in \(F\) is a sum of at most \(2^n\) squares in \(F\). knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Form Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reznick’s uniform-denominator theorem for positive-definite homogeneous forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a homogeneous form of even degree \(2d\) satisfying \(p(x)>0\) for every \(x\ne0\). Then there exists an integer \(r\ge0\) such that
\[
\left(x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2\right)^r p(x)
\]
is a sum of squares of real homogeneous polynomials. Thus the fixed positive-definite quadratic norm form supplies a denominator family that is uniform in shape: only its exponent depends on \(p\). Equivalently, \(p\) is a rational SOS whose common denominator can be chosen as \(\left(x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2\right)^{r/2}\) in the rational-function field, with parity absorbed after squaring.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive-definite even-degree form becomes SOS after multiplication by a sufficiently high power of the squared Euclidean norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Form Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the strict positivity hypothesis required by the norm-form multiplier theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A real homogeneous form \(p\) of even degree \(2d\) is positive definite precisely when
\[
p(x)>0\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}.
\]
By homogeneity, this is equivalent to strict positivity on the unit sphere. Since the sphere is compact, it is also equivalent to the existence of \(m>0\) such that
\[
p(x)\ge m\left(x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2\right)^d\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Merely assuming \(p\ge0\) permits nonzero zeros and does not satisfy this positive-definite scope condition for the stated norm-form multiplier theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Degree Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records finite uniform multiplier degree under fixed dimension, degree, and positivity margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(n,d\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(\eta\in(0,1]\). For a positive-definite form \(p\) of degree \(2d\), define
\[
\eta(p)=\frac{\min_{\|x\|_2=1}p(x)}{\max_{\|x\|_2=1}p(x)},\qquad
r_*(p)=\min\{r\ge0:(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^r p\text{ is SOS}\}.
\]
There exists a finite integer \(R(n,d,\eta)\) such that \(r_*(p)\le R(n,d,\eta)\) whenever \(\eta(p)\ge\eta\). The resulting SOS has degree at most \(2(d+R(n,d,\eta))\). No bound uniform over all positive-definite forms of fixed \(n,d\) is asserted as the positivity margin tends to zero.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Gram feasibility without a positive-definite feasible matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{A}:\mathbb{S}^N\to\mathbb{R}^M\) be the coefficient map determined by \(z_d^{\mathsf T}Qz_d\), and let \(b\) be the coefficient vector of \(p\). The Gram system is boundary feasible when \(\mathcal{F}=\{Q\in\mathbb{S}_+^N:\mathcal{A}(Q)=b\}\) is nonempty but \(\mathcal{F}\cap\mathbb{S}_{++}^N=\varnothing\). Equivalently, exact SOS Gram matrices exist, but every feasible Gram matrix is singular; hence Slater's strict-feasibility condition fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary Gram feasibility means exact positive-semidefinite Gram matrices exist, but every feasible Gram matrix is singular.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{A}\) is the Gram coefficient map for a fixed basis.
\(b\) is the exact coefficient vector of \(p\).
